items.title: p-regular and p-singular elements
p-regularity is preserved by conjugacy and by powers coprime to the element order
items.strategy: Conjugacy preserves element order, and raising an element to a power coprime to its order preserves the prime divisors of that order.

items.title: Teichmuller lift in a splitting p-modular system
The Teichmuller lift is multiplicative and unique
items.strategy: Use the unique lift of each root of unity of order prime to p inside the valuation ring unit group, and verify multiplicativity before passing to residues.

items.title: Brauer character of a finite-dimensional kG-module
The Brauer character is independent of basis and splitting-field realization
items.strategy: The multiset of eigenvalues of a p-regular element is basis-independent, and the Teichmuller lift identifies the same prime-to-p roots of unity across equivalent splitting realizations.

items.title: Brauer characters are class functions on p-regular elements
items.strategy: Conjugate matrices have the same eigenvalues, so the lifted eigenvalue sum depends only on the p-regular conjugacy class.

items.title: Brauer characters are additive on short exact sequences
items.strategy: For a p-regular element, choose a basis compatible with a submodule in a short exact sequence so the action matrix is block upper triangular, and then add the lifted diagonal eigenvalues.

items.title: Brauer-Nesbitt determines semisimplifications
items.strategy: Compare composition-factor multiplicities through Brauer characters on p-regular classes and use the splitting-system control to conclude equality of semisimplified modules.

items.title: Irreducible Brauer characters form a basis of the p-regular class functions
items.strategy: Choose a complex realization of Brauer values, extend a class function on G^0 by zero to G, decompose it into ordinary irreducible characters, and then rewrite each restricted ordinary character as the Brauer character of a modular reduction. Use the standard independence theorem for irreducible Brauer characters to conclude basis.

items.title: The number of simple kG-modules equals the number of p-regular conjugacy classes
items.strategy: Count the basis elements supplied by the irreducible Brauer characters and identify the ambient vector-space basis with p-regular conjugacy classes.

items.title: Decomposition map from ordinary to modular Grothendieck groups
The decomposition map is independent of the stable lattice
items.strategy: Compare two stable lattices by inserting powers of the uniformizer between them and use additivity of the Grothendieck-group class on the resulting short exact sequences.

items.title: Decomposition numbers and the decomposition matrix
Decomposition numbers are nonnegative integers
items.strategy: Each decomposition coefficient is a composition multiplicity in the reduction of a stable lattice, so it is an integer and cannot be negative.

items.title: Projective indecomposable characters and Cartan invariants
Brauer reciprocity
items.strategy: Lift the projective cover of a simple module to the valuation ring, compare its characteristic-zero decomposition with the reduction of a stable lattice, and identify both multiplicities with the same modular composition count.

items.title: The Cartan matrix is D^T D
items.strategy: Write each Cartan entry as a multiplicity inside a projective cover, convert those multiplicities with Brauer reciprocity, and sum over ordinary irreducibles.

items.title: p-blocks from primitive central idempotents
Blocks partition the ordinary and Brauer irreducible characters
items.strategy: Primitive central idempotents split the ordinary and modular representation categories into orthogonal summands, so each irreducible character or Brauer character lies in exactly one block.

items.title: After block ordering, the decomposition matrix is block diagonal
items.strategy: A nonzero decomposition number forces the ordinary and Brauer irreducibles to lie in the same block, so reindexing by blocks isolates independent diagonal blocks.

items.title: Defect groups and Brauer's main theorems lie beyond this page
items.strategy: Record the exact sequel boundary: this page reaches primitive central block idempotents, block partitions, and decomposition data, but defect groups, Brauer pairs, and Brauer's main theorems start on the later block-theory pages.

items.title: FALSE: a Brauer character is defined on all elements by the usual trace
items.strategy: Refute by a p-singular element whose ordinary trace exists in the defining field but does not determine a Brauer-character value because the Teichmuller-lift construction only applies on p-regular eigenvalues.

items.title: FALSE: modular representations are determined by ordinary characters
items.strategy: Refute by separating a module from its semisimplification: Brauer characters only record the composition factors, not the full extension data of a modular representation.

items.title: FALSE: reduction mod p of an ordinary irreducible is always irreducible
items.strategy: Refute inside the item with the two-dimensional ordinary irreducible of S_3 in characteristic 2: a stable lattice reduces with more than one composition factor, so an ordinary irreducible need not stay simple modulo p.

items.title: FALSE: the Cartan matrix equals the decomposition matrix
items.strategy: Refute by dimension and indexing: the Cartan matrix records projective composition multiplicities, whereas the decomposition matrix records ordinary-to-modular reduction coefficients and only determines the Cartan matrix through D^T D.

items.title: FALSE: every block has one ordinary and one Brauer irreducible character
items.strategy: Refute by contrasting defect-zero and higher-defect blocks: the block partition does not force a one-by-one decomposition block.

title: Brauer Characters and Decomposition Matrices — Examples

items.title: Brauer characters of a p-group
items.strategy: Use the fact that a finite p-group has only the trivial simple module in characteristic p, and then compute the unique irreducible Brauer character on the single p-regular class.

items.title: The p-regular classes of S_3
items.strategy: List the conjugacy classes of S_3 and separate them according to whether their element orders are divisible by the chosen prime.

items.title: The decomposition matrix of S_3 in characteristic 2
items.strategy: Compute the reduction of an integral S_3-lattice directly in characteristic 2, identify the resulting modular composition factors on the two 2-regular classes, and package those coefficients into the decomposition matrix.

items.title: Computing a Cartan matrix from D^T D
items.strategy: Take an explicit decomposition matrix, multiply D^T D, and interpret the entries as projective composition multiplicities.

items.title: A block with one ordinary and one Brauer irreducible character
items.strategy: Use a defect-zero or one-character block from the basic modular examples and verify that its block idempotent supports exactly one ordinary and one Brauer irreducible.

items.title: An ordinary trace on a p-singular unipotent element is not a Brauer-character value
items.strategy: Take a p-singular element acting unipotently in characteristic p, compute its ordinary trace, and show that this trace does not extend the Brauer character because the latter is only defined on p-regular elements.

title: Second Cohomology and Abelian Kernel Extensions

items.title: Normalized two-cocycles and two-coboundaries
Normalized two-cocycles and two-coboundaries form groups
items.strategy: Check closure, identity, and inverses under pointwise addition of cochains and use the linearity of the degree-two cocycle equation.

items.title: Second cohomology by factor sets
The factor-set model agrees with the inhomogeneous cochain model in degree two
items.strategy: Write the degree-two inhomogeneous bar differential explicitly, identify its normalized cocycles and coboundaries with the factor-set formulas on this page, and conclude that both quotient constructions are the same H^2.

items.title: Extensions inducing a prescribed abelian-kernel action
Normalized set-theoretic section and factor set
The factor set of a section is a normalized two-cocycle
items.strategy: Expand associativity of three lifted elements and read the resulting equality in the abelian kernel as the cocycle identity.

items.title: Changing the section changes the factor set by a coboundary
items.strategy: Write a second section as the first section twisted by a one-cochain and compute the new factor set term by term.

items.title: An extension determines a well-defined H^2 class
items.strategy: A section produces a normalized two-cocycle, and changing the section only changes that cocycle by a coboundary.

items.title: Twisted-product extension from a two-cocycle
The twisted product is a group exactly when the factor set is a two-cocycle
items.strategy: Check the identity and inverse formulas directly, and compare associativity of triples in M x G with the cocycle equation term by term.

items.title: Cohomologous two-cocycles give equivalent extensions
items.strategy: A one-cochain defines the middle-group isomorphism (m, g) -> (m + c(g), g) between twisted products, and the converse reads an extension equivalence back into the same formula.

items.title: H^2 classifies extensions with fixed abelian kernel action
items.strategy: Construct the two maps between extension classes and H^2 by passing from a section to its factor set and from a cocycle to its twisted product, and prove they are inverse under the fixed action and equivalence conventions.

items.title: The zero H^2 class is equivalent to a split extension
items.strategy: The zero cocycle produces the semidirect product, and a split extension yields a normalized section with trivial factor set after the classification theorem is unwound.

items.title: Baer sum of abelian-kernel extensions
Baer sum is independent of extension representatives
items.strategy: Equivalent extensions give isomorphic pullbacks and pushouts, so the pullback-then-pushout construction depends only on the extension class.

items.title: Baer sum agrees with addition in H^2
items.strategy: Choose normalized sections on the two extensions, compute the factor set of the pullback/pushout model, and identify it with the pointwise sum of the original cocycles.

items.title: Central extensions are classified by H^2 with trivial action
items.strategy: Centrality is exactly the triviality of the induced action, so the general H^2 classification specializes immediately.

items.title: Extension-theoretic interpretation of the standard five-term exact sequence
items.strategy: Interpret inflation and restriction through the published degree-one maps and identify the transgression with the obstruction class attached to extending a complement or section across the given abelian-kernel extension.

items.title: Nonabelian extension obstructions live in H^3
items.strategy: Record the sequel boundary: fixed-action abelian-kernel extensions are classified by H^2 here, whereas nonabelian kernels require an obstruction in H^3 and only yield an H^2-torsor when that obstruction vanishes.

items.title: FALSE: every function G x G -> M is a factor set
items.strategy: Refute by checking that an arbitrary function need not satisfy the normalized cocycle equation required for associativity of the twisted product.

items.title: FALSE: the factor set is independent of the chosen section as a function
items.strategy: Refute by changing a section by a nontrivial one-cochain and observing that the resulting cocycle changes by the corresponding two-coboundary.

items.title: FALSE: H^2 classifies extensions with arbitrary nonabelian kernel
items.strategy: Refute by distinguishing the abelian-kernel classification proved here from the nonabelian-kernel obstruction theory recorded in the remark boundary.

items.title: FALSE: equivalent extensions only require the middle groups to be isomorphic
items.strategy: Refute by recalling that extension equivalence fixes both the kernel and quotient identifications; an abstract isomorphism of middle groups does not suffice.

items.title: FALSE: the zero H^2 class corresponds to the direct product only
items.strategy: Refute by noting that the zero class yields the semidirect product for the fixed action, which is a direct product only in the trivial-action case.

title: Second Cohomology and Abelian Kernel Extensions — Examples

items.title: The C_p^2 extension as a nonzero two-cocycle
items.strategy: Write C_{p^2} as an extension of C_p by C_p, choose the obvious set-theoretic section, and compute the resulting normalized cocycle to show that the class is nonzero.

items.title: The split extension arises from the zero cocycle
items.strategy: Use the zero factor set in the twisted-product construction and identify the resulting middle group with the semidirect product for the given action.

items.title: Central extensions of a cyclic group
items.strategy: For a cyclic quotient and trivial action, compute representative cocycles and identify the corresponding split and nonsplit central extensions.

items.title: Quaternion and dihedral central extension classes
items.strategy: Compare the central extension classes that yield dihedral and quaternion groups and read their difference as a distinct H^2 class.

items.title: Changing a section by a one-cochain
items.strategy: Modify a chosen normalized section by a concrete one-cochain and compute the resulting change in the factor set as the corresponding two-coboundary.

items.title: Baer sum of two factor sets
items.strategy: Take two explicit cocycles for the same action, add them, and compare the resulting twisted product with the pullback/pushout Baer-sum construction.

items.title: The same middle group can support inequivalent extension structures
items.strategy: Put different kernel and quotient identifications on one abstract middle group and show that no extension equivalence fixes both ends simultaneously.
